items.followUp: Differentiate between alcoholic fermentation and aerobic respiration.

rubric.why: Identifies the characteristic products of alcoholic fermentation.
rubric.description: States that alcoholic fermentation produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly linking ethanol and carbon dioxide with alcoholic fermentation.

rubric.why: Identifies the characteristic product of lactic acid fermentation.
rubric.description: States that lactic acid fermentation produces lactic acid, for example in muscle cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying lactic acid as the product.

modelAnswer: Alcoholic fermentation: In the absence of oxygen, yeast converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide.
Lactic acid fermentation: In the absence of oxygen, glucose is converted into lactic acid, as in muscle cells.

items.followUp: What is the difference between ATP and ADP in energy storage?

rubric.why: Shows the role of ATP in providing or transferring energy for cell activities.
rubric.description: States that ATP is the cell’s energy currency or supplies energy for cellular work.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an accurate role of ATP.

rubric.why: Identifies the subject studied by bioenergetics.
rubric.description: Defines bioenergetics as the study of energy transformations in living organisms.

modelAnswer: ATP stores and transfers energy and is the immediate energy source for cellular activities.
Bioenergetics is the study of energy transformations in living organisms.

items.followUp: Explain oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer.

rubric.why: Gives a valid definition of oxidation.
rubric.description: Defines oxidation as loss of electrons, addition of oxygen, or removal of hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one correct definition of oxidation.

rubric.why: Gives a valid definition of reduction.
rubric.description: Defines reduction as gain of electrons, removal of oxygen, or addition of hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one correct definition of reduction.

modelAnswer: Oxidation is the loss of electrons, addition of oxygen, or removal of hydrogen.
Reduction is the gain of electrons, removal of oxygen, or addition of hydrogen.

items.followUp: What is meant by the active site of an enzyme?

rubric.why: Shows that enzyme action is selective rather than general.
rubric.description: States that an enzyme acts on a specific substrate or catalyses a particular reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the enzyme’s specificity.

rubric.why: Connects enzyme specificity with the matching substrate and active site.
rubric.description: Explains that only a substrate with a suitable fit binds to the enzyme’s active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the specific fit between enzyme and substrate.

modelAnswer: An enzyme is specific: it acts only on a particular substrate or catalyses a particular reaction.
This specificity occurs because only the appropriate substrate fits the enzyme’s active site.

items.followUp: Describe how the enzyme-substrate complex is formed and broken down.

rubric.why: States the central idea of the lock-and-key model.
rubric.description: Explains that the substrate fits the enzyme’s active site because their shapes are complementary, like a key in a lock.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the matching substrate and active-site shapes.

rubric.why: Describes what happens after the substrate binds.
rubric.description: States that an enzyme-substrate complex forms, products are released, and the enzyme remains unchanged.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing complex formation and product release with the enzyme unchanged.

modelAnswer: In the lock-and-key model, the enzyme’s active site has a specific shape complementary to its substrate, like a lock to a key.
The substrate binds to form an enzyme-substrate complex; products are released and the enzyme remains unchanged.

items.followUp: What is a bivalent, and during which stage of meiosis does it form?

rubric.why: Identifies which chromosomes pair and when synapsis occurs.
rubric.description: States that synapsis is the pairing of homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying the pairing and its stage.

rubric.why: Names the structure formed by the paired homologous chromosomes.
rubric.description: States that the paired homologous chromosomes form a bivalent (tetrad).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the resulting structure.

modelAnswer: Synapsis is the pairing of homologous chromosomes along their lengths during prophase I of meiosis.
The paired chromosomes form a bivalent, also called a tetrad.

items.followUp: Give two examples each of plant macronutrients and micronutrients.

rubric.why: Distinguishes macronutrients by the amount required by the plant.
rubric.description: States that macronutrients are required in relatively large amounts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the amount required.

rubric.why: Distinguishes micronutrients by amount and gives relevant examples, or gives examples of macronutrients alongside their definition.
rubric.description: States that micronutrients are required in small amounts and gives examples such as iron or zinc; examples of macronutrients include nitrogen and phosphorus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the micronutrient definition with an example, or appropriate examples of macronutrients.

modelAnswer: Macronutrients are plant nutrients required in relatively large amounts, for example nitrogen and phosphorus.
Micronutrients are required in small amounts, for example iron and zinc.

rubric.why: Identifies the form in which water is lost during transpiration.
rubric.description: States that water is lost as water vapour.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying water vapour as the substance lost.

rubric.why: Identifies the route of stomatal transpiration.
rubric.description: States that the water vapour passes out through the stomata, usually of leaves.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying stomata as the route.

modelAnswer: Stomatal transpiration is the loss of water from a plant as water vapour through the stomata, mainly in the leaves.
